items: Heap = unordered 8 KB pages; seq scan reads all of them
Selectivity of `WHERE` does not shrink a seq scan
Index = separate structure mapping key values to TIDs
`ctid` = block number + item offset inside that block
Postgres has secondary indexes only, no InnoDB-style clustered store

blocks.title: Indexes You Already Have
items: One implicit index per `PRIMARY KEY`
One per `UNIQUE` constraint
`FOREIGN KEY` columns get none
Classic cause of slow cascading deletes
Bitmap scan builds a TID bitmap, then sorts it
Heap then read in physical order, not random order
Combines several indexes with bitmap AND / OR
Planner picks by estimated cost, never by rules
Index wins under roughly 5-10% row selectivity
Above that, random I/O dominates and seq scan is cheaper
On SSD set `random_page_cost = 1.1` or index use stays suppressed

blocks.title: Where Selectivity Comes From
items: `pg_statistic`, refreshed by `ANALYZE`
`n_distinct`, `most_common_vals` / `freqs`
`histogram_bounds` for ranges
`correlation` for physical order
Compare `rows=` estimated against actual rows
A 100x gap means stale statistics, not a missing index
`Rows Removed by Filter` = index fetched rows then threw them away
That index simply is not selective enough

blocks.title: Index Cond, Not Filter
blocks.text: `Index Cond` is evaluated inside the index; `Filter` runs after the heap fetch. Moving a predicate from Filter to Index Cond is the whole game.

lines: -- a failed build leaves an INVALID index
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx;  -- then retry

blocks.title: Indexes Charge Writes
blocks.text: Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` must maintain every index on the table.

items: Default index type in Postgres
Balanced multi-way tree, all leaves at the same depth
Typically 3-4 levels for hundreds of millions of rows
Fanout ~ page_size / entry_size
8 KB pages, 3 levels, billions of keys addressed
So a lookup costs about 4 page reads
Leaf pages are doubly linked left to right (Lehman & Yao)
Range and backward scans walk siblings, never revisit the root
Right-links let readers proceed during a page split
No tree-wide locks needed for concurrency
A full page splits about 50/50
Rightmost inserts split 90/10 for monotonic keys
`serial` and `now()` hit that path constantly
`fillfactor` default 90 leaves 10% for HOT-friendly growth
Lower it on heavily updated indexes

blocks.title: Modern Shrinkage
items: PG 13+ deduplication: one key, a posting list of TIDs
Low-cardinality indexes shrink dramatically
PG 14+ bottom-up deletion reclaims dead entries before splitting
Fights version churn from non-HOT updates
Index tuples carry no `xmin` / `xmax`
So heap or visibility map must be consulted
Entries exist for dead tuples too
Only `VACUUM` removes them

lines: WHERE a IS NULL          -- yes, indexed

blocks.title: 2704 Bytes Max
blocks.text: Entries cap at ~1/3 of a page; long text raises `index row size exceeds maximum`. Hash the value or index an expression instead.

slides.page_title: B-tree in Practice: Multicolumn, Order, Sorting

items: Multicolumn keys are compared left to right
Only a leftmost prefix can become an `Index Cond`
A skipped leading column ends index usability

lines: CREATE INDEX ON t (a, b, c);
WHERE a=1 AND b=2 AND c=3 -- served

items: For `WHERE a = 1 AND b > 5 ORDER BY c`, two candidates exist
Index `(a, b)` stops the scan at `b`
Index `(a, c)` bounds `a` and gives the sort for free
Measure both, do not guess
A range predicate ends usable index ordering
Columns after the first inequality become filters, not bounds

left.title: two single-col indexes
items: column order irrelevant
bitmap AND of both
extra bitmap step

right.title: one composite index
items: prefix order matters
single index scan
nearly always faster

lines: CREATE INDEX ON t (a DESC, b ASC);
-- ORDER BY a DESC, b ASC : no Sort node

items: `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` must match the query's `ORDER BY`
B-tree does store NULLs, unlike Oracle
So `WHERE col IS NULL` can use an index scan

lines: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC

items: Row comparison `(a, b) > (1, 2)` maps to a composite bound
The expanded `OR` rewrite usually does not
`text_pattern_ops` / `varchar_pattern_ops` enable `LIKE 'abc%'`
Needed whenever the collation is not C
`COLLATE "C"` on the column achieves the same
A glibc upgrade changing `lc_collate` silently corrupts text ordering
`REINDEX` after any collation version change

blocks.title: Housekeeping
items: Index `(a)` is redundant beside `(a, b)`
Drop the narrow one unless small and hot
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` enforces uniqueness
NULLs are distinct; `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) forbids repeats

lines: CREATE INDEX ON pages USING hash (url);
WHERE url = $1   -- the only served op

items: Stores a 32-bit hash code, never the value itself
Index size is independent of the column's data width
A 4 KB URL and a 20-byte slug cost the same
Lookup is O(1) expected: hash, jump to bucket, scan the page
Bucket splits happen incrementally as the index grows
No single giant rehash pause
Before PG 10 hash indexes were not WAL-logged
Unsafe after a crash and never replicated
PG 10+ made them crash-safe and replicable
No `ORDER BY`, ranges or `LIKE`
No uniqueness, primary keys or exclusion constraints
One column only, never multicolumn
No index-only scan: the value is unrecoverable from the hash

blocks.title: Always Rechecked
blocks.text: Hash collisions are possible, so Postgres compares the real value against the heap tuple on every hit.

items: Real win: very long equality keys, URLs, long text ids
Exactly where a btree entry is huge or breaks the size limit
Otherwise btree lands within a few percent and stays flexible

blocks.title: Same Trick, Cheaper Hash
items: `hashtext(long_col)` also works as an expression index
Query predicate must repeat the function exactly
Gives ordering and index-only scans that hash cannot
GIN = Generalized Inverted Index
For column types holding many elements
Arrays, `jsonb`, `tsvector`, trigrams
Answers 'which rows contain this element'
Exact inverse of btree's 'which rows equal this value'

slides.page_title: GIN: Inverted Index for Composite Values

lines: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin

items: `jsonb_path_ops` is much smaller and faster, containment only
Arrays: `WHERE tags @> ARRAY['pg']` is GIN-accelerated
So is `&&` overlap between two arrays
`pg_trgm` also makes `ILIKE` and fuzzy `%` similarity indexable
One row touches many index keys, so writes are slow
`fastupdate` buffers inserts in a pending list
Flushed in batches, so an occasional query pays the cost
A big pending list has to be scanned linearly

lines: -- 4MB is the default; lower to flush often
-- caps rows from very common terms

blocks.title: Lossy, Always
blocks.text: GIN results are rechecked against the heap every time, so index-only scans are impossible with GIN.

items: Not for range queries and not for sorting
Reach for it on containment, overlap and text search

blocks.title: Before A Big Build
items: Raise `maintenance_work_mem` first
It dominates GIN build speed
Restore it after the build finishes
GiST = Generalized Search Tree, a balanced tree framework
The data type supplies the behaviour, not the index
Internal nodes store a lossy summary of their subtree
A search descends every branch whose summary might match

blocks.title: Methods The Type Supplies
items: `consistent` and `union`
`penalty` and `picksplit`
`same`
Lossy summaries make results approximate
Every candidate row is rechecked against the heap
Unlike btree, subtree regions may overlap
Search follows multiple paths, so worst case is data-dependent

lines: ALTER TABLE booking ADD EXCLUDE USING gist
-- no double-booking; btree cannot do this

items: `btree_gist` lets scalar types join a GiST index
So an equality column sits beside a range column
Both live in one exclusion constraint

lines: -- no full sort of the table

items: `gist_trgm_ops` is smaller and faster to build than GIN
But slower to search, so GIN wins read-heavy text
GiST updates are cheaper than GIN's
Prefer GiST when the column is written often
Space-Partitioned GiST: unbalanced, non-overlapping partitions
Quadtrees, k-d trees and radix tries
Excels at point data and `inet` addresses
Also text prefix search, where partitions never overlap
BRIN = Block Range INdex
Stores min/max per range of heap blocks, not per row
`pages_per_range` defaults to 128, so one tuple covers 1 MB
Index size is tiny, often thousands of times under btree
Lossy by design: never proves a row matches
Only proves a block range might match
So it is always a bitmap heap scan, never a plain index scan

lines: CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (ts);

items: Canonical fit: append-only time-series with a `created_at`
Or a log table with a monotonically increasing id
Anti-pattern: a `uuid` or hashed key, randomly distributed
There every range matches, degenerating into a seq scan plus overhead
Lower `pages_per_range` = more precision, bigger index
Raise it for very large, very well-correlated tables
New ranges are summarized on `VACUUM`
Or force it with `brin_summarize_new_values('idx')`
`autosummarize = on` handles it automatically

caption.text: Most slow Postgres queries already have an index — it just is not the one the planner can use. This handbook opens up btree, hash, GIN, GiST and BRIN from the inside: page splits, posting lists, block summaries, visibility bits, and the exact reason `WHERE date(created_at) = ...` throws your index away. Ten pages, from the cost constants to the workflow that turns a Filter into an Index Cond.
